tier_reason: The paper (arXiv 1910.05109, published in Software: Practice and Experience 50(2), 2020) benchmarks the AVX-512 codec against the Chrome base64 library. It states GCC 9.1 with -O3 -march=cannonlake and an Intel i3-8121U (Cannon Lake). The benchmark code is public in the linked repo: src/benchmark.c and the Makefile, which builds chromiumbase64, fastavxbase64 and the AVX-512 VBMI codecs with -O3 -march=cannonlake.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper conclusion: 'our codec is 10 to 20 times faster than a highly optimized conventional codec' (Chrome). The AVX-512 codec is limited to ~40 GB/s for inputs larger than 16 kB (in L2), against Chrome's 1.5 GB/s encode and 2.6 GB/s decode. Table 3 gives real-file decode at 25-42 GB/s for AVX-512 vs 2.6 GB/s for Chrome. The 'over 150 GB/s' figure is memcpy's top speed in L1 (~10 kB inputs), not the codec's.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i3-8121U (Cannon Lake, 2018), 2.2 GHz base / 3.2 GHz max, 32 kB L1d per core (paper Table 2)

notes: Everything checks out except two points. The 150 GB/s figure was attributed to the codec but is actually the memcpy peak. The hardware field lacked the CPU model, now added. License BSD-3-Clause, 206 stars and last commit 2019-11-19 (abandoned) all verified via gh.

tier_reason: The README benchmark log puts const_hex against the hex crate (plus rustc_hex, faster_hex and std formatting) in the same run. It states rustc 1.83.0-nightly (9ff5fc4ff 2024-10-03) and an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X. The numbers came from the libtest benches in benches/bench/main.rs at commit ce406b5 (2024-10-06). At that commit Cargo.toml had no [profile] override, so the flags are the default cargo bench profile (opt-level=3).
notes: The benchmark_url pointed at the 'main' branch, which returns 404; the default branch is master. The license is dual MIT OR Apache-2.0 (Cargo.toml and README), although gh reports only Apache-2.0. The README numbers date from 2024-10 and were produced with the old libtest harness, but the benches have used divan since 2025-06. Page data gives ratios up to ~99x at 1MB encode (derived from page data) and ~158x for 1MB std formatting (derived from page data), above the README's '10 to 50 times' phrasing.

tier_reason: The README table (Old vs New MB/s, 2.09x-2.35x at 1kB-32kB) names the CPU (AMD Ryzen 9 9950X), and the benchmark code is public: BenchmarkCRC32 in crc32_test.go. Neither the README nor PR #20 states the Go toolchain version or the go test command and flags. 'Based on Go 1.24' describes the source base, and go.mod declares only go 1.23.0. Under the orchestrator's Go rule that makes these first-party numbers C, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. The README says the library is 'based on Go 1.24' (the source base) and go.mod declares go 1.23.0. The benchmark names (BenchmarkCRC32/...-32) indicate go test -bench with default settings, but no command or toolchain version is given.
corrections.caveats: 'Old' is the regular SSE4.1/PCLMULQDQ implementation (the README calls it 'the regular SSE4 implementation'), not AVX2. PR #20's first commit is 'Use latest go src as base', so Old is effectively the Go standard library hash/crc32 code, and New adds AVX-512 on top. AVX-512 turns on only above 1KB, and PR #20 shows ~1.00x at 15B, 40B and 512B. There is no comparison against zlib's C crc32(). The Go toolchain version is unstated.

notes: The numbers match the README and PR #20 exactly. The 'prior (SSE4/AVX2)' wording was wrong: the baseline is the upstream Go stdlib SSE4.1/PCLMULQDQ path. Metadata verified via gh: BSD-3-Clause (Go license), 84 stars, last commit 2025-07-22, stale.
